title: AP Computer Science Principles
summary: Explore program design, data, algorithms, networks and computing impacts.
frameworkNote: Unit map checked against College Board on 15 October 2026 for the 2026-27 course. Each unit has one focused original revision lesson, not exhaustive topic coverage or an official practice paper. The official framework uses five Big Ideas rather than numbered units. Includes revision of concepts relevant to the Create task, not a submission or replacement for independently authored assessed work.

modules.title: Iterative development with observable tests
modules.focus: Turn a user need into a testable behaviour.
explanation: A program’s purpose describes the problem it addresses; its behaviour describes what it does for particular inputs. Iterative development cycles through design, implementation, testing and revision, using feedback to refine a concrete requirement.

An abstraction hides details behind a useful interface, such as a procedure with parameters. Good tests specify inputs and expected outputs before execution. Collaboration can reveal assumptions, but each contribution and reused source should be acknowledged.

workedExample.prompt: A library reminder tool should flag loans more than 14 days old. Design a boundary test.
steps: Choose loan ages 13, 14 and 15 to distinguish below, at and above the threshold.
Expected flags are false, false and true because the requirement says more than 14.

misconception.claim: A program that runs without crashing must meet its purpose.
misconception.correction: Logical errors can produce wrong results without any runtime failure.

questions.prompt: A requirement says discounts apply at age 65 or older. Give two boundary tests.
questions.hint: Use the boundary and the value just below it.
questions.answer: Age 64 should not qualify; age 65 should qualify.

questions.prompt: Why use a parameterised calculateTotal(prices) procedure?
questions.answer: It hides repeated summation details and can process different price lists through one interface.

questions.prompt: A rule allows at most five attempts. Give boundary tests for attempts already used 4,5,6 if another attempt is allowed only when fewer than five have been used.
checkpoints: Five or six used meets or exceeds the limit.
hints: Another attempt requires used<5.
Four used leaves one available.

questions.hint: A one-element list would not expose the error.
questions.prompt: A total(prices) procedure incorrectly returns the first price. Give a smallest nonempty list that exposes the error and the expected output.
questions.answer: For [2,3], the expected total is 5, not 2.
checkpoints: A one-element list would not expose the error.
Sum both entries to define the oracle.
hints: A one-element list would not expose the error.
Use two nonzero values.

notes.title: Reasoning through iterative development with observable tests
paragraphs: A requirement describes externally observable behaviour, while an implementation describes how that behaviour is produced. Tests become stronger when their expected outputs are decided from the requirement before running the code. Boundary cases expose ambiguity in phrases such as above, at least and no more than. Iteration uses test evidence to refine both code and requirements. A procedure can hide repeated details behind a meaningful interface, but its parameters and return value still need clear meanings. Passing a few tests supports those cases; it does not prove correctness for every possible input.

workedExamples.prompt: A delivery rule charges 4 units for baskets below 30 and zero otherwise. Design three tests.
steps: Choose basket values 29,30,31 around the threshold.
Expected fees are 4,0,0 because 30 qualifies.
A failing test at 30 would expose use of > rather than ≥.
workedExamples.conclusion: The tests distinguish the exact boundary rule.

flashcards.front: What makes a test oracle useful?
flashcards.back: It specifies the expected result independently of the implementation.

flashcards.front: Why test the exact threshold?
flashcards.back: It distinguishes strict from inclusive comparisons.

flashcards.front: What is procedural abstraction?
flashcards.back: Encapsulating details behind a named operation with an interface.

flashcards.front: Do passing examples prove universal correctness?
flashcards.back: No.

modules.title: Bits, compression and meaningful data
modules.focus: Separate a representation from its interpretation.
explanation: With n bits there are 2^n possible patterns. Interpreting those patterns requires a scheme: the same bits could encode numbers, characters or image information. Increasing bit depth increases representational possibilities, not necessarily the accuracy of an original measurement.

Lossless compression permits exact reconstruction, whereas lossy compression discards some information. Combining datasets can reveal new patterns but may also expose private information through linkage. Check missing values and collection methods before treating a pattern as a population fact.

workedExample.prompt: How many distinct values can an unsigned 5-bit field represent, and what is its largest value?
steps: Five binary positions give 2⁵=32 patterns.
Counting from zero gives values 0 through 31, so the largest is 31.

misconception.correction: Lossless compression preserves the information needed for exact reconstruction.

questions.prompt: How many bits are needed to encode at least 100 distinct categories?
questions.hint: Find the smallest power of two at least 100.

questions.prompt: A medical image must be reconstructed exactly. Which compression type fits that requirement?
checkpoints: Exact reconstruction is the deciding requirement.

questions.prompt: What is the minimum bit count for 17 distinct symbols?
hints: Four bits provide only 16 patterns.
Five bits provide 32 patterns.

questions.hint: Pixel count is width times height.
questions.prompt: An image doubles both width and height at fixed bits per pixel. How does uncompressed pixel storage change?
checkpoints: Pixel count is width times height.
Each dimension contributes a factor of 2.
Bits per pixel remain unchanged, so total scales by 4.
hints: Pixel count is width times height.
Each dimension contributes a factor of 2.

notes.title: Reasoning through bits, compression and meaningful data
paragraphs: Bits represent patterns; meaning comes from the agreed encoding. The same pattern can represent a number, colour or character under different conventions. An n-bit unsigned integer has 2ⁿ possible patterns and a maximum value of 2ⁿ−1. Increasing precision or resolution usually increases storage requirements. Lossless compression reconstructs the original exactly, whereas lossy compression deliberately removes information according to a model of acceptable change. A smaller file is not automatically a better representation: scientific measurements and editable originals may require details that a viewing-focused format discards.

workedExamples.prompt: An uncompressed image has 20×10 pixels and 3 bytes per pixel. Find its data size, ignoring metadata.
steps: There are 200 pixels.
Each requires 3 bytes, so storage is 600 bytes.
Multiply by 8 to express the same size in bits.
workedExamples.conclusion: The pixel data occupy 600 bytes or 4,800 bits.

flashcards.front: How many patterns do n bits support?
What is the largest unsigned n-bit integer?
What does lossless compression guarantee?
flashcards.back: Exact reconstruction of the original data.

flashcards.front: Why does interpretation need an encoding?
flashcards.back: The bits alone do not specify their meaning.

modules.title: Algorithms, lists and procedural abstraction
modules.focus: Trace a list algorithm and explain its general behaviour.
explanation: An algorithm is a finite, ordered procedure for a task. Sequencing, selection and iteration can express a wide range of algorithms. A list groups related values so one loop can process different amounts of data without separate variables for every item.

Efficiency compares resource use as input size grows. A linear search may inspect every element, while binary search repeatedly halves a sorted search range. A simulation models assumptions; its results are only as applicable as those assumptions.

workedExample.prompt: Trace an algorithm that starts total at zero and adds only values greater than 3 from [2,5,3,7].
steps: 2 and 3 fail the strict condition; 5 and 7 pass.
The accumulated total is 5+7=12.

misconception.claim: A simulation guarantees the real system will behave identically.
misconception.correction: It estimates behaviour under a model whose assumptions require checking.

questions.prompt: How many list elements can a linear search inspect in the worst case for a list of 20?
questions.hint: The sought value may be absent.

questions.prompt: For list [1,4,6], an algorithm doubles each value then keeps values above 8. What remains?
questions.hint: Apply the operations in the stated order.

questions.prompt: Trace count=0; for each x in [4,4,1,7], increment count when x≥4.
checkpoints: Count occurrences rather than distinct values.
hints: Both occurrences of 4 qualify.
1 fails and 7 qualifies.

questions.prompt: An ordered list has 32 entries. Under repeated halving, how many halvings reduce a candidate interval of 32 to size 1?
checkpoints: Each step divides the candidate count by 2.
hints: Track sizes 32,16,8,4,2,1.
Each step divides the candidate count by 2.

notes.title: Reasoning through algorithms, lists and procedural abstraction
paragraphs: An algorithm is a finite, unambiguous process expressed through sequencing, selection and iteration. A list can let one procedure handle many data items without a separate variable and instruction for each. Trace state changes after each element rather than jumping directly to an intuition about the final answer. Searching and sorting have different costs and requirements: binary search needs ordered data and repeatedly narrows an interval, while linear search works without that ordering. An abstraction reduces detail for its caller, but correctness still depends on preserving the procedure’s stated input and output behaviour.

workedExamples.prompt: Trace a procedure that starts result at 1 and multiplies it by each odd number in [2,3,4,5].
steps: 2 is even, so result stays 1.
3 is odd, so result becomes 3; 4 is skipped.
5 is odd, so result becomes 15.

flashcards.front: What are three basic algorithm control structures?
flashcards.back: Sequence, selection and iteration.

flashcards.front: What precondition does binary search require?
flashcards.back: The searched data must be ordered consistently.

flashcards.front: Why initialise a product to 1?
flashcards.back: One is the multiplicative identity.

flashcards.front: What benefit does a list provide?
flashcards.back: A uniform way to process a variable number of related items.

modules.title: Packets and redundant paths
modules.focus: Explain how network design tolerates some failures.
explanation: The internet connects networks using shared protocols. Data can be broken into packets whose routes differ; packet routing does not guarantee that every packet arrives in its original order. Higher-level protocols can support reassembly and reliable delivery.

Redundant connections create alternative routes when some links fail. They improve resilience but do not guarantee immunity to every failure. Parallel computing divides suitable work across processors, although sequential parts and coordination overhead limit speedup.

workedExample.prompt: A network has routes A-B-D and A-C-D. If link B-D fails, can A still reach D?
steps: The first route is broken because one required link is unavailable.
The route A-C-D remains, so communication can continue if those links operate.

misconception.claim: Adding processors always halves the execution time.
misconception.correction: Only parallelisable work benefits; sequential work and overhead remain.

questions.prompt: A job takes 2 seconds of sequential work plus 8 seconds that divide perfectly over four processors. Find ideal total time.
Why can packets arrive out of order?
questions.answer: They may travel along different routes or encounter different delays.
checkpoints: Distinguish sending order from arrival order.
Mention reconstruction by the receiving protocol.

questions.hint: Both routes start at A and end at D.
questions.prompt: A network has paths A-B-D and A-C-D. Which single endpoint failure certainly prevents A communicating with D?
checkpoints: Both routes start at A and end at D.
Intermediate alternatives do not replace either endpoint.
Endpoint availability is required for communication.
hints: Both routes start at A and end at D.
Intermediate alternatives do not replace either endpoint.

questions.prompt: A task has 5 seconds sequential work and 15 seconds ideally parallelisable work. Find the best possible limiting time as processor count grows without bound.
checkpoints: The parallel term tends to zero.
hints: Write T(p)=5+15/p.
The parallel term tends to zero.

notes.title: Reasoning through packets and redundant paths
paragraphs: Packet switching divides messages into smaller units that can share links with other traffic. Packets may experience different delays and arrive out of order; higher-level protocols can handle sequencing and retransmission where required. Redundant routes improve resilience only when failures do not remove every path between endpoints. The internet’s routing function differs from a web application running over it. Parallel processing also has limits: work that must remain sequential sets a floor on total execution time, even if the parallel portion has ideal speedup and communication overhead is ignored.

workedExamples.prompt: A task takes 3 seconds sequentially and 12 seconds of perfectly parallel work. Find ideal time on 3 and 6 processors.
steps: With 3 processors, the parallel portion takes 12/3=4 seconds, so total is 7.
With 6 processors it takes 2 seconds, so total is 5.
The sequential 3 seconds cannot be divided in this model.
workedExamples.conclusion: Ideal totals are 7 and 5 seconds; doubling processors does not halve total time.

flashcards.front: Why can packet order change?
flashcards.back: Different routes and queue delays can produce different arrival times.

flashcards.front: What does route redundancy provide?
flashcards.back: Alternative paths when some links fail.

flashcards.front: What limits ideal parallel speedup?
flashcards.back: The portion that must remain sequential.

flashcards.front: Is the web identical to the internet?
flashcards.back: No; it is a service using internet infrastructure.

modules.title: Computing impacts and biased samples
modules.focus: Evaluate benefits alongside who is excluded.
explanation: Computing systems can distribute benefits and harms unevenly. A digital divide can arise from access, cost, connectivity, language or accessibility barriers. Identifying an affected group makes an impact claim more useful than saying technology is simply good or bad.

An algorithm can reproduce bias in its training data or objective even when it executes exactly as written. Privacy review considers what data is collected, how long it is retained and who can access it. A security measure should address a particular threat.

workedExample.prompt: A bus-planning app learns routes only from smartphone volunteers. Identify a possible bias.
steps: People without smartphones cannot contribute, so their travel needs may be underrepresented.
The recommended routes may favour the sampled group; broader sampling could test and reduce that gap.

misconception.claim: Correct code is necessarily fair code.
misconception.correction: Fairness depends on data, goals, design and effects as well as implementation accuracy.

questions.prompt: Why can collecting precise location when only city totals are needed increase privacy risk?
questions.answer: It exposes more about individual movement than the stated analysis requires.
checkpoints: Connect it to potential identification or tracking.

questions.prompt: What does multifactor authentication add beyond a password?
questions.hint: Think about independent evidence of identity.
questions.answer: A second factor, such as possession of a device, reduces reliance on the password alone.
checkpoints: Do not claim it removes every threat.

questions.prompt: A route app needs neighbourhood totals but stores precise home coordinates. Give a concrete data-minimisation change and its benefit.
questions.answer: Aggregate to neighbourhood counts and avoid retaining precise homes when unnecessary.
checkpoints: Exact coordinates exceed that stated need.
Reducing retained precision lowers exposure of household locations.
hints: The purpose requires neighbourhood-level totals.
Exact coordinates exceed that stated need.

questions.hint: The current sample omits the deployment condition.
questions.prompt: A model is tested only on daytime images but will operate at night. Identify the evaluation gap and a direct test.
questions.answer: Nighttime performance is unknown; evaluate a labelled nighttime sample representative of intended use.
checkpoints: The current sample omits the deployment condition.
Daytime success does not establish nighttime accuracy.
Measure errors on relevant nighttime cases.
hints: The current sample omits the deployment condition.
Daytime success does not establish nighttime accuracy.

notes.title: Reasoning through computing impacts and biased samples
paragraphs: A computing system can produce unequal outcomes because of its data, objective, design or deployment context. Measuring average accuracy alone can hide errors concentrated in a smaller group. Data minimisation asks whether each collected field is necessary for the stated purpose; removing names does not always prevent re-identification when detailed records can be linked. Evaluate a system with the people affected, and distinguish a measured disparity from an established explanation for it. A useful mitigation has a testable effect and acknowledged trade-offs rather than a claim that one technical change removes every social concern.

workedExamples.prompt: A classifier is correct for 90 of 100 group-A cases and 50 of 100 group-B cases. Calculate overall and group accuracies.
steps: Group A accuracy is 90%; group B is 50%.
Across all cases, 140 of 200 are correct, giving 70%.
The average conceals a 40-percentage-point group gap.
workedExamples.conclusion: Report both the 70% overall accuracy and the separate group results.

flashcards.front: Why inspect subgroup results?
flashcards.back: Overall averages can hide concentrated errors.

flashcards.front: Does deleting names ensure anonymity?
flashcards.back: No; other fields can enable linkage.

flashcards.front: What is data minimisation?
flashcards.back: Collecting only information needed for the stated purpose.

flashcards.front: Does disparity alone prove its cause?
flashcards.back: No; causal explanation needs further evidence.
